source: BED-LLM (ICLR 2026): choosing queries by expected information gain, Table 1
finding: In 20 Questions, picking questions by an EIG computed from the LLM's own hypothesis samples and answer likelihoods beat letting the LLM pick questions. The LLM itself supplies prior and likelihood; no settings were handed over.
numbers: Success rate %, 3 problem sets x 6 LLMs. Animals GPT-4o: Prompt-Only 45, CoT 62, Split 83, BED-LLM 93. Things Llama-3.1-8B: 10 vs 26. Mean over all 18 cells of Table 1: BED-LLM minus Prompt-Only = 40.4 pp (paper abstract says 37.4 pp; the gap is not explained in the text I read). Standard errors about 2.2-5.0.
quote: improves the success rate by 37.4 percentage points compared to direct prompting
limits: Closed game with a fixed answer list; hypotheses and candidate questions come from the LLM, the answerer is an LLM. No token-matched comparison in the main table.
agent_relevance: Supports a test-design step that samples hypotheses, asks what each predicts, and scores candidate tests by the spread of predicted answers. Gap 1 answered in part: the LLM can write its own likelihood.

finding: A cheap version where the LLM just picks the best of the same candidate questions (Implicit Maximization) helps a little. The full EIG helps much more. Marginal-entropy only (Entropy) sits in between.
numbers: Averages over the 18 Table 1 cells (my arithmetic, unweighted): Implicit Max minus Prompt-Only = +8.2 pp; BED-LLM minus Implicit Max = +32.2 pp; BED-LLM minus Split (deterministic likelihood) = +15.3 pp. Entropy ablation e.g. Celebrities GPT-4o 64 vs BED-LLM 86.
limits: Standard errors per cell about 3-5 pp.
agent_relevance: Telling the model to pick the most informative test from a list gives little. An explicit score over sampled hypotheses gives most of the gain. Compute informativeness, do not assert it.

source: BED-LLM appendix: static vs updating likelihood, run time
finding: Letting the likelihood depend on the whole chat history made results worse in most cells. BED-LLM run time is about equal to Entropy and Split; Prompt-Only and CoT are cheapest; Data-Estimation is over 10x slower.
numbers: Table 4: Animals GPT-4o 93 static vs 86 updating; Celebrities Qwen2.5-72B 84 vs 70; Celebrities Llama-3.3-70B 55 vs 44; a few cells slightly better with updating (Animals Llama-3.1-8B 63 vs 67). Only one wall-clock value legible in the text extraction: 26m 29s (Qwen2.5-72B, whole Animals set; method not recoverable).
limits: No token-matched Prompt-Only with extra samples was run, so gap 1 (equal budget) stays open. Cost is shown as time, not tokens.
agent_relevance: Keep the test-scoring model fixed rather than re-asking it with history in context (context shifts calibration).

source: Huang et al. POPPER: Table 3 Type-I error and power
finding: Sequential falsification with e-values kept Type-I error near alpha=0.1 on two of three sets and above it on TargetVal-IFNG. Baselines without error control were often above alpha.
numbers: Table 3 (5 runs, mean +- sd). POPPER Type-I: DiscoveryBench 0.152+-0.031, TargetVal-IL2 0.016+-0.014, IFNG 0.180+-0.028; power 0.610, 0.897, 0.717. ReAct Type-I 0.145 / 0.020 / 0.004, power 0.378 / 0.140 / 0.040. Self-Refine Type-I 0.248 on DiscoveryBench. POPPER-CodeGen (no relevance check) Type-I 0.311 / 0.264 / 0.173. Paper's control rule: alpha within 1 sd of the result.
limits: Earlier claim K16 said POPPER stays below alpha; 0.152 and 0.180 are above 0.1 and pass only by the 1-sd rule. IL2/IFNG have only 20 positives and 50 permuted nulls. Author list not checked.
agent_relevance: Error control comes from the stopping rule plus a relevance check, not from the LLM. A falsification loop needs a preset alpha and a check that each test really tests the claim.

source: POPPER backbone table, failure shares, human comparison
finding: Weak models break the error control. Most failures are misreading p-values or poor test choice, not hallucination. The agent matched nine human experts in Type-I and power.
numbers: Table 4: GPT-4o Type-I 0.230 on DiscoveryBench; o1 0.143, power 0.730; Claude Haiku 3.5 high Type-I. Failure shares: misread p-values 35.9%, ineffective experiment design 28.1%, test breaks implication 17.2%, wrong implementation 8.6%, hallucination 0.8%. Nine biologists: no significant difference; POPPER 9.7x faster, 3.6x more code lines, 2.5x more tests. Relevance checker vs human: Spearman 0.55 (p=5e-6); labelled 85% of proposals strongly implied vs human 77%.
limits: Nine humans is small. Error categories were LLM-labelled then human-checked.
agent_relevance: Failures are mostly in reading statistics and design, so the check step should review the step from p-value to claim, not only whether code runs.

finding: All Type-I numbers use random column-wise permutation nulls. No non-permutation null (a real but irrelevant dataset, a confounded null) was tested. The authors say Type-I control does not imply discoveries are true.
numbers: DiscoveryBench: as many permuted negatives as positives; TargetVal: 50 negatives for 20 positives.
limits: Gap 4 half closed: real table numbers checked (d04, d05). Whether control holds on non-permutation nulls is untested.
agent_relevance: A permutation null destroys structure that could fool the agent. Use harder seeded nulls (confounded, near-miss) when testing our own test loop.

source: Starace et al. PaperBench: stage-wise scores (Table 9)
finding: Agents write code far better than they run it or analyse results. Same pattern in every model.
numbers: Replication score by requirement type, BasicAgent: Claude-3.5-Sonnet code development 35.4, execution 1.8, results analysis 0.7. o1: 19.5 / 5.7 / 0.0. o3-mini: 5.1 / 0.6 / 0.4. 4o: 7.7 / 0.1 / 0.0. o1 IterativeAgent: 43.3 / 4.5 / 0.0; o1 36-hour: 42.4 / 7.4 / 1.4.
limits: Execution and analysis requirements are graded by an LLM judge on artifacts; near-zero partly means the agent never ran the code. Early-2025 models.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 only in part: the weak stage is run-and-read. No study here varied a forced run-and-check step alone.

finding: Removing the early-stop option and prompting piecemeal work raised o1 and o3-mini but lowered Claude. Authors saw that all models except Claude often stopped early, claiming to be done or stuck.
numbers: BasicAgent to IterativeAgent: o3-mini-high 2.6 to 8.5; o1-high 13.2 to 24.4; Claude-3.5-Sonnet 21.0 to 16.1. 36-hour o1 26.0. Code-Dev o1 43.4.
limits: Stopping and prompt changed together. Authors say the prompt is tuned for o-series. Claude 3.7 not run (rate limits).
agent_relevance: Gap 9: a cheap predictor is the model's early-finish rate in a plain run (authors' observation, not a tested rule).

source: PaperBench human baseline over time (Fig. 3, Section 5.4)
finding: o1 beats the human baseline in the first hours, plateaus, and humans win after about 24 hours.
numbers: 8 ML PhD participants, 4-paper subset, 3 attempts per paper, best of 3; 4-week window; o1 run 36 h with snapshots graded at 1, 3, 6, 12, 36 h.
limits: Tiny human sample; participants chose papers.
agent_relevance: More agent time stops paying early; later gains need a changed plan, not more of the same.

source: Kon et al. EXP-Bench: Table 1 and failure analysis
finding: Whole-experiment success is near zero. Failures are mostly missing parts of the implementation and broken environments.
numbers: 461 tasks, 51 papers. OpenHands + o3-mini: All 1.4, All-and-executable 0.5 (420 runs). Claude-3.7 Sonnet: All 0.7, All+E 0.4 (235 runs). Failure shares: missing essential implementation components 39.71%, environment or dependency misconfiguration 29.38%, script-level issues 23.8%. Cost per run: 3.7 Sonnet median $7.53 (mean $10.15) vs o3-mini median $0.35; about 25-34 min mean.
limits: Tasks built semi-automatically from papers; LLM monitor grades. Columns as printed: D, I, E, I-and-E, C, All, All-and-E.
agent_relevance: Supports K11 with two benchmarks. Cost varies about 20-30x across models at similar All scores.

finding: The forced-continue scaffold did not help the two small models tested. It lowered the D and C columns and whole-task score stayed 0.
numbers: IterativeAgent Claude-3.5 Haiku: D 6.4 (OpenHands 20.6), C 2.2 (13.8), All 0.0; E 25.2 (OpenHands 9.3). IterativeAgent Nova Pro: D 0.1 (18.2), C 0.3 (15.7), All 0.0. Haiku mean time 30 min, max 403 min.
limits: Different scaffold family (OpenHands vs IterativeAgent), small models. Not the PaperBench setting.
agent_relevance: Second case that forced continuation depends on the model. Prefer a stop rule tied to a check, not to time.

source: Nadgir et al. Life After Benchmark Saturation: CORE-Bench v1.1 (June 2026)
finding: On CORE-Bench Hard top agents reached 97.4-100% and could not be ranked by accuracy. Log review found 15 task errors and 20 tasks with exploitable shortcuts; fixed set has 39 tasks (v1.1) plus a 19-task out-of-distribution set.
numbers: v1.1: Codex CLI GPT-5.3-Codex 97.4%, GPT-5.4 high 97.4%, GPT-5 84.6%; Claude Code Opus 4.6 92.3%. Codex CLI beat the CORE-Agent scaffold by about 44 pp on GPT-5.4 medium. OOD set: GPT-5.2 100%, GPT-5.4 low 84.2%. Human-agent trial: 20 papers, completion time more than halved; one-fifth of human-only sessions hit the 3-hour limit.
limits: Small suites, wide intervals. Task is reproducing given code, not running new experiments.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: the can't-run-code failure has largely gone for reproducing existing repos by mid-2026, but scaffold still moves results by tens of points. The older 21.5% Hard figure is out of date.

finding: Five Codex CLI agents re-run five more times. More accurate agents were more consistent. Stated confidence was far below success and did not separate right from wrong.
numbers: Mean pass rate 93% vs mean stated confidence 32.1%. Confidence tracked bash error count, but that count was uncorrelated with success; no agent beat random guessing at telling correct from incorrect runs.
limits: Post-hoc verbal confidence from an extra prompt; five agents.
agent_relevance: Do not take the agent's own confidence as a sign a test result is sound. Use an external check (executed output, known-answer case).

source: Thomas, Gligoric, Shah: Mitigating LLM-based p-hacking by preregistering for the next LLM
finding: Fixing the analysis plan before the run, and running it on a model released after the plan, would have blocked most p-hacks in LLM-analysis pipelines. A preregistered test confirmed it.
numbers: 20 models, 4 providers, 11 configurations, two tasks with known truth (AI-text share in pre-LLM peer reviews, true 0%; calories day 1 vs day 2, true 50%). Hacked cells 23 and 44; blocked 17 of 23 (73.9%, Wilson 95% CI 53.5-87.5) and 32 of 44 (72.7%, CI 58.2-83.7). Own preregistered test: 6 of 7 hacked configurations failed to carry to the next model.
limits: Researchers tuning LLM labelling, not an autonomous agent. About a quarter of hacks still transferred. Needs a future model, which an agent cannot get.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: direct evidence that locking the plan blunts hack transfer, but not a test of an agent fixing its own pass criterion. Nearest in-session version: fix the criterion, then check on held-out items or a different model.

source: Vaccaro: Preregistration for Experiments with AI Agents (ICML 2026 position paper)
finding: Lists the researcher degrees of freedom in LLM experiments and offers a template. A specification-curve simulation shows how much the choices move results.
numbers: 2,430 specifications on LLM anchoring (model family, system prompt, anchor distance, delivery, question content, outlier handling) gave indices from strongly negative to strongly positive: one path could report human-like, none or reverse anchoring.
limits: Position paper; shows spread, not a measured p-hacking rate.
agent_relevance: The agent should log every analytic choice and report the spread, not one path.

source: Luo, Kasirzadeh, Shah: The More You Automate, the Less You See
finding: Two open AI scientist systems (Agent Laboratory, AI Scientist v2) were tested in controlled setups with known truth. Found benchmark-selection bias, undocumented synthetic data or subsampling, and an internal reward that sees test scores and favours them.
numbers: Agent Laboratory: 945 and 927 explicit benchmark selections in 1,000 runs per setting; 82.4% chose among the first four listed (with SOTA reference). AI Scientist v2: control picks top-ranked candidate 82.0%; with test results inverted it chose the lowest-ranked about half the time (never in control). Leakage test: labels flipped at 20% and 30% so the ceiling is 1 minus noise; accuracy above the ceiling counts as peeking. Neither system read test data directly.
limits: Two systems, ML tasks only. No deliberate metric cherry-picking found, only arbitrary metric choice.
agent_relevance: Seeded-truth injection with a known ceiling is an evaluator-side calibration and it caught problems. Gap 3 partly answered: it works for auditing agents, but no study puts it inside an agent's own loop.

source: Luo et al.: auditing from logs vs paper only
finding: An LLM auditor finds these flaws much better from trace logs and code than from the final paper.
numbers: Overall: paper only accuracy 55.0%, F1 0.51; paper plus logs plus code accuracy 85.0%, F1 0.86 (about 20 cases per cell). Post-hoc selection bias: paper only F1 0.31, with logs F1 0.90.
limits: Auditor is an LLM; sample about 20 per cell.
agent_relevance: Matches the Sakana finding: a good-looking write-up does not show sound testing. Keep the test log as the thing to check.

source: Aher, Arriaga, Kalai: Using LLMs to simulate multiple humans and replicate human subject studies
finding: Four classic studies were simulated: Ultimatum Game, garden-path sentences, Milgram, wisdom of crowds. The first three replicated with recent models; wisdom of crowds showed hyper-accuracy.
numbers: Larger models more faithful. Authors changed details of three of four studies to reduce recall of memorised versions.
limits: All four are famous classics; no comparison with later real replications. Gap 10 stays open: no evidence that simulations predict outcomes of unseen replications.
agent_relevance: Do not use simulated subjects to decide whether a claim replicates.

source: Original texts of Hacking, Galison, Gooding (gap 7)
finding: Not opened this session. WebSearch budget ran out and the arXiv, OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar APIs returned HTTP 429, so no book text was reached.
limits: Gap 7 stays open; claims K01-K03 and K22 still rest on the encyclopedia summary.
